claim: P-TEFb phosphorylates Ser2 residues of the C-terminal domain (CTD) of the largest subunit (RPB1) of RNA polymerase II.
source: The Positive Transcription Elongation Factor b (P-TEFb) phosphorylates Ser2 residues of the C-terminal domain (CTD) of the largest subunit (RPB1) of RNA polymerase II and is essential for the transition from transcription initiation to elongation in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of P-TEFb.

claim: P-TEFb is essential for the transition from transcription initiation to elongation in vivo.
source: The Positive Transcription Elongation Factor b (P-TEFb) phosphorylates Ser2 residues of the C-terminal domain (CTD) of the largest subunit (RPB1) of RNA polymerase II and is essential for the transition from transcription initiation to elongation in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about P-TEFb function.

claim: P-TEFb exhibits Ser5 phosphorylation activity in vitro.
source: Surprisingly, P-TEFb exhibits Ser5 phosphorylation activity in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Tyr1 phosphorylation directs the kinase activity of P-TEFb and alters its specificity from Ser5 to Ser2.
source: Through in vitro reconstruction of CTD phosphorylation, mass spectrometry analysis, and chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) analysis, we uncover a mechanism by which Tyr1 phosphorylation directs the kinase activity of P-TEFb and alters its specificity from Ser5 to Ser2.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including mass spectrometry, immunoblotting, and ChIP-seq.

claim: The loss of Tyr1 phosphorylation causes an accumulation of RNA polymerase II in the promoter region.
source: The loss of Tyr1 phosphorylation causes an accumulation of RNA polymerase II in the promoter region as detected by ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript showing increased pausing index upon inhibition of Tyr1 phosphorylation.

claim: Tyr1 phosphorylation generates a heterogeneous CTD modification landscape that expands the CTD's coding potential.
source: We demonstrate the ability of Tyr1 phosphorylation to generate a heterogeneous CTD modification landscape that expands the CTD's coding potential.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data showing different phosphorylation patterns when Tyr1 is phosphorylated.

claim: Previously installed modifications direct the identity and abundance of subsequent coding events by influencing the behavior of downstream enzymes.
source: These findings provide direct experimental evidence for a combinatorial CTD phosphorylation code wherein previously installed modifications direct the identity and abundance of subsequent coding events by influencing the behavior of downstream enzymes.
evidence: This is the interpretation of the experimental findings showing that Tyr1 phosphorylation affects P-TEFb specificity.

claim: The CTD is composed of a species-specific number of repeats of the consensus amino acid heptad YSPTSPS.
source: The C-terminal domain of the RPB1 subunit of RNA polymerase II (CTD) is composed of a species-specific number of repeats of the consensus amino acid heptad YSPTSPS (arbitrarily numbered as Tyr1, Ser2, Pro3, Thr4, Ser5, Pro6, and Ser7) (Jeronimo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: The CTD undergoes extensive post-translational modification that recruits RNA processing and transcription factors.
source: The CTD undergoes extensive post-translational modification (PTM) that recruits RNA processing and transcription factors that regulate progression through the various stages of transcription.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CTD function.

claim: The major sites of phosphorylation in the CTD are Ser5 and Ser2.
source: The major sites of phosphorylation are Ser5 and Ser2, directed by Transcription Factor II H (TFIIH) (Feaver et al., 1994) and P-TEFb in mammals (Marshall et al., 1996), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: TFIIH directs phosphorylation of Ser5.
source: The major sites of phosphorylation are Ser5 and Ser2, directed by Transcription Factor II H (TFIIH) (Feaver et al., 1994) and P-TEFb in mammals (Marshall et al., 1996), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: P-TEFb directs phosphorylation of Ser2 in mammals.
source: The major sites of phosphorylation are Ser5 and Ser2, directed by Transcription Factor II H (TFIIH) (Feaver et al., 1994) and P-TEFb in mammals (Marshall et al., 1996), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: In mammalian cells, the phosphorylations of Tyr1 and Ser7 rise and peak near the promoter along with Ser5.
source: In mammalian cells, the phosphorylations of Tyr1 and Ser7 rise and peak near the promoter along with Ser5 and gradually decrease as transcription progresses towards termination.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the temporal dynamics of CTD phosphorylation.

claim: The phosphorylation of Thr4 and Ser2 appear later in the transcription cycle during elongation.
source: The phosphorylation of Thr4 and Ser2, on the other hand, don't appear until later in the transcription cycle during elongation (Eick and Geyer, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: P-TEFb is overexpressed in multiple tumor types.
source: P-TEFb is of particular interest due to its overexpression in multiple tumor types and role in HIV infection (Franco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: P-TEFb plays a role in HIV infection.
source: P-TEFb is of particular interest due to its overexpression in multiple tumor types and role in HIV infection (Franco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: P-TEFb promotes transcription by contributing to the release of RNA polymerase II from the promoter-proximal pause through its phosphorylation of NELF, DSIF, and Ser2 of the CTD.
source: As a major CTD kinase, P-TEFb promotes transcription by contributing to the release of RNA polymerase II from the promoter-proximal pause through its phosphorylation of Negative Elongation Factor (NELF), DRB Sensitivity Inducing Factor (DSIF), and Ser2 of the CTD (Wada et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: P-TEFb phosphorylates Ser5 of the CTD in vitro.
source: Interestingly, P-TEFb seems to phosphorylate Ser5 of the CTD in vitro and mutation of Ser5 to alanine prevents the phosphorylation of CTD substrates.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and confirmed by the authors' experiments.

claim: Mutation of Ser5 to alanine prevents the phosphorylation of CTD substrates by P-TEFb.
source: Interestingly, P-TEFb seems to phosphorylate Ser5 of the CTD in vitro and mutation of Ser5 to alanine prevents the phosphorylation of CTD substrates. However, mutation of Ser2 to alanine did not result in this abolishment (Czudnochowski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Mutation of Ser2 to alanine does not prevent phosphorylation of CTD substrates by P-TEFb.
source: However, mutation of Ser2 to alanine did not result in this abolishment (Czudnochowski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Compromised P-TEFb kinase activity results in a specific reduction in levels of Ser2 phosphorylation in vivo.
source: These results are in contrast to in vivo studies of P-TEFb specificity, where compromised P-TEFb kinase activity results in a specific reduction in levels of Ser2 phosphorylation (Marshall et al., 1996).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: P-TEFb generates two phospho-peptides when phosphorylating unmodified yeast CTD: a major species phosphorylated on Ser5 and a minor species phosphorylated on Ser2.
source: With high kinase and ATP concentration (2 mM) and overnight incubation (~16 hr), P-TEFb generates two phospho-peptides as detected by LC-UVPD-MS/MS: a major species phosphorylated on Ser5 (Y1S2P3T4pS5P6S7) and a minor species phosphorylated on Ser2 (S5P6S7Y1pS2P3T4) (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by LC-UVPD-MS/MS data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: P-TEFb's phosphorylation pattern on unmodified CTD is highly similar to patterns observed for Ser5 CTD kinases Erk2 and TFIIH.
source: This is highly similar to patterns observed previously for bona fide Ser5 CTD kinases Erk2 and TFIIH (Mayfield et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published data.

claim: P-TEFb adds 24 to 29 phosphates to yeast CTD's 26 heptad repeats.
source: MALDI-MS analysis of yCTD treated with P-TEFb reveals a cluster of peaks with mass shifts relative to no kinase control ranging from 1906.1 to 2318.4 Da, each interspaced by 80 Da (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C). This corresponds to the addition of 24 to 29 phosphates to yCTD's 26 heptad repeats.
evidence: This is supported by MALDI-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: P-TEFb phosphorylates the CTD in an average one phosphorylation per heptad manner, and these heptads are primarily phosphoryl-Ser5 in vitro.
source: This finding in combination with our LC-UVPD-MS/MS analysis of P-TEFb treated yCTD indicates that P-TEFb phosphorylates the CTD in an average one phosphorylation per heptad manner, and these heptads are primarily phosphoryl-Ser5 (pSer5) in vitro.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined MALDI-MS and LC-UVPD-MS/MS data.

claim: Conservative mutation of the Tyr1 position to phenylalanine in both Saccharomyces cerevisiae and human cells is lethal.
source: As evidence of this, even conservative mutation of the Tyr1 position to phenylalanine in both Saccharomyces cerevisiae and human cells is lethal, highlighting the significance of residue identity at this position (Hsin et al., 2014; West and Corden, 1995).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Mutating the Tyr1 position to alanine prevents phosphorylation at other CTD residues by CTD kinases.
source: Secondly, we have shown that mutating the Tyr1 position to alanine prevents phosphorylation at other CTD residues by CTD kinases (Mayfield et al., 2017), indicating the side chain at this position is important for kinase activity.
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: Phosphoryl-Tyr1 is detected at the initiation of transcription in human cells.
source: Third, phosphoryl-Tyr1 (pTyr1) is detected at the initiation of transcription in human cells (Descostes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: All three kinases (Erk2, TFIIH, and P-TEFb) are active against the phenylalanine-substituted CTD construct.
source: Unlike alanine substitution, all three kinases are active against the phenylalanine-substituted CTD construct (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The substitution of phenylalanine at the Tyr1 position alters the behavior of phosphorylated substrates in EMSA.
source: Surprisingly, the substitution of phenylalanine at the Tyr1 position alters the behavior of phosphorylated substrates in EMSA (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is observed in EMSA data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Erk2 shows a 2.5-fold higher specificity constant against the YtoF variant compared to the WT construct.
source: Erk2 shows a 2.5-fold higher specificity constant against the YtoF variant, as indicated by kcat/Km, compared to the WT construct (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TFIIH activity is greatly compromised when Tyr1 is replaced by phenylalanine with a nearly 10-fold reduction in kcat/Km.
source: However, TFIIH activity is greatly compromised when Tyr1 is replaced by phenylalanine with a nearly 10-fold reduction in kcat/Km (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: c-Abl readily phosphorylates yeast CTD in vitro.
source: C-Abl readily phosphorylates yCTD in vitro as evidenced by EMSA and detection of Tyr1 phosphorylation using pTyr1 specific antibody 3D12 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA and western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: c-Abl phosphorylates consensus CTD sequences on Tyr1 in vitro.
source: These mass shifts confirm c-Abl phosphorylates consensus CTD sequences on Tyr1 in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by LC-UVPD-MS/MS data showing phosphorylation on tyrosine residues.

claim: Imatinib decreases pTyr1 epitope abundance in a dose-dependent manner in HEK293T cells.
source: Imatinib decreases pTyr1 epitope abundance to 88.0% (10μM imatinib, not significant), 65.2% (20μM imatinib), and 51.3% (30μM imatinib) relative to paired vehicle controls.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: c-Abl phosphorylates approximately half of the available Tyr1 residues in yeast CTD.
source: High-resolution MALDI-MS spectra of samples treated by c-Abl revealed peaks accounting for yCTD containing 5 to 13 phosphates (with mass shifts ranging from 398.9 to 1049.4 Da) (Figure 2D), approximately half of yCTD's available tyrosine residues within 26 heptad repeats.
evidence: This is supported by MALDI-MS data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: c-Abl does not phosphorylate consensus CTD in every heptad; instead, it favors phosphorylation of approximately half the available Tyr1 residues.
source: These mass shifts suggest c-Abl does not phosphorylate consensus CTD in every heptad; instead, it favors phosphorylation of approximately half the available Tyr1 residues.
evidence: This is supported by MALDI-MS data from multiple CTD constructs of different lengths.

claim: Tandem treatment of yCTD with c-Abl followed by P-TEFb results in the addition of a total of 16 to 26 phosphates.
source: Interestingly, tandem treatment of yCTD with c-Abl followed by P-TEFb resulted in the addition of a total of 16 to 26 phosphates as detected by MALDI-MS, with a mass shifts of 1287.3 to 2073.2 Da (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by MALDI-MS data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: c-Abl pre-treatment results in changes to P-TEFb's phosphorylation along the CTD, evidenced by a reduction in the number of phosphate groups added by P-TEFb.
source: These data reveal c-Abl pre-treatment results in changes to P-TEFb's phosphorylation along the CTD, evidenced by a reduction in the number of phosphate groups added by P-TEFb.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MALDI-MS data comparing tandem treatment to individual treatments.

claim: Pre-treatment of yCTD with c-Abl results in a significant increase in Ser2 phosphorylation of nearly 300% by P-TEFb.
source: Compared to a non-phosphorylated CTD, the pre-treatment of yCTD with c-Abl results in a significant increase in Ser2 phosphorylation of nearly 300%, as detected by pSer2 specific CTD antibody 3E10, accompanied by a small and statistically non-significant decrease in pSer5 installed by P-TEFb (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Tandem treatment of yCTD by c-Abl followed by either TFIIH or Erk2 showed no changes in pSer2 levels.
source: The increase of pSer2 is unique for P-TEFb-mediated phosphorylation of CTD since a similar tandem treatment of yCTD by c-Abl followed by either TFIIH or Erk2 showed no changes in pSer2 levels (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claim: The increase in the apparent Ser2 phosphorylation is not due to P-TEFb's physical interaction with c-Abl but arises from c-Abl kinase activity against CTD substrates at Tyr1.
source: Therefore, the increase in the apparent Ser2 phosphorylation is not due to P-TEFb's physical interaction with c-Abl but arises from c-Abl kinase activity against CTD substrates at Tyr1.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that inactivation of c-Abl before P-TEFb addition still results in increased Ser2 phosphorylation.

claim: When treated with P-TEFb alone, di-heptads with both Ser5 residues phosphorylated are the predominant product.
source: Double phosphorylated species are also detected for di-heptads with both Ser5 residues phosphorylated as the predominant product (Figure 3E and F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, peak 5).
evidence: This is supported by LC-UVPD-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The most abundant species from tandem phosphorylation with c-Abl followed by P-TEFb contains both Tyr1 and Ser2 phosphorylation.
source: The most abundant of these unique species (Figure 3G peak 7) contains both Tyr1 and Ser2 phosphorylation (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by LC-UVPD-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: In di-heptads with Tyr1 phosphorylated, Ser2 becomes the primary target of P-TEFb phosphorylation.
source: Our results show that in di-heptads with Tyr1 phosphorylated, Ser2 becomes the primary target of P-TEFb phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by LC-UVPD-MS/MS data comparing phosphorylation patterns with and without c-Abl pre-treatment.

claim: When the S5A construct is treated with c-Abl followed by P-TEFb, up to seven phosphates are added to the final product.
source: Subsequent treatment with P-TEFb results in an obvious shift in the MALDI-MS spectra with up to seven phosphates added to the final product (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is supported by MALDI-MS data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Upon Tyr1 phosphorylation, S5A becomes a viable substrate for P-TEFb and adds at least two additional phosphates likely to Ser2 residues.
source: The results corroborate the conclusion drawn from the MS/MS results, indicating that upon Tyr1 phosphorylation S5A becomes a viable substrate for P-TEFb and adds at least two additional phosphates likely to Ser2 residues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MALDI-MS data from the S5A construct experiments.

claim: TFIIH-mediated phosphorylations do not alter P-TEFb specificity in vitro.
source: These data indicate that TFIIH-mediated phosphorylations do not alter P-TEFb specificity in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by LC-UVPD-MS/MS data showing that TFIIH pre-treatment does not change P-TEFb's preference for Ser5.

claim: Treatment of HEK293T cells with 10 µM dasatinib results in a reduction in pTyr1 of 30%, accompanied by a 29% decrease in Ser2 phosphorylation.
source: At 10 µM dasatinib, pTyr1 levels are reduced by 30% in HEK293T cells, and this is accompanied by a 29% decrease in Ser2 phosphorylation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Treatment of HEK293T cells with 20 μM imatinib results in a reduction in pTyr1 of 35%, accompanied by a statistically significant decrease in pSer2 levels of 15%.
source: Treatment of HEK293T cells with 20 μM imatinib results in a reduction in pTyr1 of 35%. This is accompanied by a statistically significant decrease in pSer2 levels of 15% (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In both the dasatinib and imatinib treatments, pSer5, POLR2A, and POLR2C levels remain unaffected.
source: In both the dasatinib and imatinib treatments pSer5, POLR2A, and POLR2C levels remain unaffected (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: The distribution of RNA polymerase II along the gene body is altered in multiple genes upon dasatinib treatment.
source: In comparison of the dasatinib treated cells with the vehicle controls, the distribution of RNA polymerase II along the gene body is altered in multiple genes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A significant increase of peak height for RNA polymerase II was found in the promoter region of many genes upon dasatinib treatment.
source: Signal was normalized to 10M reads for both samples, and a significant increase of peak height for RNA polymerase II was found in the promoter region of many genes, as demonstrated in representative genes Myc and FANCL (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A statistically significant increase close to two-fold in pausing index can be observed in G2 and G3 genes upon inhibition of Tyr1 phosphorylation.
source: But a statistically significant increase can be observed close to two-fold in G2 and G3 genes (Figure 5C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: RNA polymerase II is stalled in the promoter region upon the inhibition of Tyr1 phosphorylation.
source: Overall, these results suggest that RNA polymerase II is stalled in the promoter region upon the inhibition of Tyr1 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ChIP-seq data showing increased pausing index.

claim: The discovery that Tyr1 phosphorylation of the CTD alters the preference of P-TEFb from Ser5 to Ser2 resolves the controversy surrounding P-TEFb's specificity.
source: Our discovery that Tyr1 phosphorylation of the CTD alters the preference of P-TEFb from Ser5 to Ser2 resolves the controversy surrounding P-TEFb's specificity (Bartkowiak et al., 2010; Czudnochowski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings in the context of previous literature.

claim: P-TEFb was initially identified as a CTD kinase that controls the elongation potential of RNA polymerase II.
source: P-TEFb was initially identified as a CTD kinase that controls the elongation potential of RNA polymerase II, is required for the majority of RNA polymerase II transcription, and is specific for Ser2 in vivo (Chao and Price, 2001; Marshall et al., 1996; Ni et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: P-TEFb is required for the majority of RNA polymerase II transcription.
source: P-TEFb was initially identified as a CTD kinase that controls the elongation potential of RNA polymerase II, is required for the majority of RNA polymerase II transcription, and is specific for Ser2 in vivo (Chao and Price, 2001; Marshall et al., 1996; Ni et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: P-TEFb is incapable of phosphorylating Ser2 of CTD peptides in vitro.
source: However, these early conclusions are at odds with in vitro data demonstrating P-TEFb is incapable of phosphorylating Ser2 of CTD peptides in vitro (Czudnochowski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: CDK12 and CDK13 display Ser2 kinase activity in cells but do not seem to play a major role in Ser2 phosphorylation in early transcriptional events.
source: Two other kinases, CDK12 and CDK13, display Ser2 kinase activity in cells but do not seem to play a major role in Ser2 phosphorylation in early transcriptional events (Bartkowiak et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Continuous heptad repeats with phosphorylated pTyr1 inhibit subsequent CTD modification by P-TEFb.
source: It should be stressed that continuous heptad repeats with phosphorylated pTyr1 inhibit subsequent CTD modification by P-TEFb (Czudnochowski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: When treated biochemically with c-Abl, the pTyr1 pattern not only allows for P-TEFb phosphorylation but also shifts the substrate preference from Ser5 to Ser2.
source: However, when treated biochemically with c-Abl, the pTyr1 pattern not only allows for P-TEFb phosphorylation but also shift the substrate preference from Ser5 to Ser2.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental data.

claim: Inhibition of Tyr1 phosphorylation leads to the reduction of Ser2 phosphorylation in human cells.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of Tyr1 phosphorylation leads to the reduction of Ser2 phosphorylation in human cells and the accumulation of Pol II in the promoter-proximal pausing stage of transcription.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' experimental data from inhibitor treatments and ChIP-seq.

claim: Inhibition of Tyr1 phosphorylation leads to the accumulation of Pol II in the promoter-proximal pausing stage of transcription.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of Tyr1 phosphorylation leads to the reduction of Ser2 phosphorylation in human cells and the accumulation of Pol II in the promoter-proximal pausing stage of transcription.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' ChIP-seq data.

claim: Tyr1 phosphorylation has been implicated in stabilizing RNA polymerase II in cells.
source: Tyr1 phosphorylation has been implicated in stabilizing RNA polymerase II in cells (Hsin et al., 2014), transcription termination (Mayer et al., 2012) and anti-sense transcription (Descostes et al., 2014) but a coherent molecular basis for these disparate functions remains elusive.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Tyr1 phosphorylation has been implicated in transcription termination.
source: Tyr1 phosphorylation has been implicated in stabilizing RNA polymerase II in cells (Hsin et al., 2014), transcription termination (Mayer et al., 2012) and anti-sense transcription (Descostes et al., 2014) but a coherent molecular basis for these disparate functions remains elusive.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Tyr1 phosphorylation has been implicated in anti-sense transcription.
source: Tyr1 phosphorylation has been implicated in stabilizing RNA polymerase II in cells (Hsin et al., 2014), transcription termination (Mayer et al., 2012) and anti-sense transcription (Descostes et al., 2014) but a coherent molecular basis for these disparate functions remains elusive.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The ability of Tyr1 phosphorylation to redirect signaling and influence subsequent modifications along the CTD suggests various roles for pTyr1 may arise indirectly.
source: The ability of Tyr1 phosphorylation to redirect signaling and influence subsequent modifications along the CTD, as revealed for P-TEFb, suggests these various roles for pTyr1 may arise indirectly.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: Tyr1 phosphorylation is relatively transient, appearing at the transition from initiation to elongation and decreasing rapidly through the action of phosphatase(s).
source: Tyr1 phosphorylation is relatively transient, appearing at the transition from initiation to elongation and decreasing rapidly through the action of phosphatase(s) (Eick and Geyer, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: pTyr1 is positioned in a vital window to alter P-TEFb specificity and regulate its phosphorylation pattern along RNA polymerase II.
source: Despite this transient nature, pTyr1 is positioned in a vital window to alter P-TEFb specificity and regulate its phosphorylation pattern along RNA polymerase II.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on their findings and the known timing of Tyr1 phosphorylation.

claim: P-TEFb is ubiquitously important for transcription across eukaryotic cells.
source: P-TEFb is ubiquitously important for transcription across eukaryotic cells and often co-opted in disease states like HIV infection and cancer (Franco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: P-TEFb is often co-opted in disease states like HIV infection and cancer.
source: P-TEFb is ubiquitously important for transcription across eukaryotic cells and often co-opted in disease states like HIV infection and cancer (Franco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: Cross-talk between CTD modification enzymes increases the diversity and coding potential of CTD heptads.
source: Overall, our findings support a model in which cross-talk between CTD modification enzymes increases the diversity and coding potential of CTD heptads.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: c-Abl phosphorylates CTD in vitro.
source: Three lines of evidence support this notion: c-Abl phosphorylates CTD in vitro (Baskaran et al., 1993) and in cells since transient over-expression of c-Abl in primate COS cells results in increased Tyr1 phosphorylation (Baskaran et al., 1997), and c-Abl immunoprecipitates with RNA polymerase II (Baskaran et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Transient over-expression of c-Abl in primate COS cells results in increased Tyr1 phosphorylation.
source: Three lines of evidence support this notion: c-Abl phosphorylates CTD in vitro (Baskaran et al., 1993) and in cells since transient over-expression of c-Abl in primate COS cells results in increased Tyr1 phosphorylation (Baskaran et al., 1997), and c-Abl immunoprecipitates with RNA polymerase II (Baskaran et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: c-Abl immunoprecipitates with RNA polymerase II.
source: Three lines of evidence support this notion: c-Abl phosphorylates CTD in vitro (Baskaran et al., 1993) and in cells since transient over-expression of c-Abl in primate COS cells results in increased Tyr1 phosphorylation (Baskaran et al., 1997), and c-Abl immunoprecipitates with RNA polymerase II (Baskaran et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Residues at the first position of the heptad are highly conserved across species.
source: First, residues at this first position of the heptad are highly conserved across species and substitution to non-aromatic residues is rare, suggesting significance to function (Chapman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Substitution of Tyr1 to non-aromatic residues is rare.
source: First, residues at this first position of the heptad are highly conserved across species and substitution to non-aromatic residues is rare, suggesting significance to function (Chapman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Erk2 is a recently identified Ser5 CTD kinase that phosphorylates primed RNA polymerase II in developmental contexts.
source: We generated GST-CTD constructs containing a portion of D. melanogaster CTD (residues 1671–1733, containing nine heptad repeats) of either tyrosine containing wild-type (dmCTD) or with phenylalanine substitution at the Tyr1 position in all nine heptads (dmCTDYtoF) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). The CTD variants purified from these constructs were phosphorylated with one of three established CTD kinases: Erk2, a recently identified Ser5 CTD kinase that phosphorylates primed RNA polymerase II in developmental contexts (Tee et al., 2014);
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The kinase module of TFIIH installs Ser5 and Ser7 marks in vivo.
source: the kinase module of TFIIH that install Ser5 and Ser7 marks in vivo (Feaver et al., 1994);
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Imatinib has potent and specific inhibition against c-Abl and ABL2.
source: Imatinib has potent and specific inhibition against c-Abl and ABL2 (which shares 93% sequence identity in the kinase domain as c-Abl) (Salah et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: ABL2 shares 93% sequence identity in the kinase domain with c-Abl.
source: Imatinib has potent and specific inhibition against c-Abl and ABL2 (which shares 93% sequence identity in the kinase domain as c-Abl) (Salah et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Controlling the kinase activity of c-Abl, or highly similar kinases, is sufficient to significantly modulate the level of Tyr1 phosphorylation of CTD in mammalian cells.
source: Overall, our result indicates controlling the kinase activity of c-Abl, or highly similar kinases, is sufficient to significantly modulate the level of Tyr1 phosphorylation of CTD in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the imatinib treatment data.

claim: Dasatinib has potent and specific inhibition against c-Abl and other tyrosine kinases similar to c-Abl.
source: Therefore, we initially utilized the potent inhibitor dasatinib, which inhibits c-Abl as well as other tyrosine kinases similar to c-Abl, to treat HEK293T cells (Winter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Tyr1 phosphorylation can block recognition of pSer2 by the 3E10 antibody.
source: One potential concern is antibody masking by flanking phosphorylation because Tyr1 phosphorylation can block recognition of pSer2 by the 3E10 antibody (Chapman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Ultraviolet photodissociation (UVPD) using 193 nm photons results in a greater number of diagnostic fragment ions and the conservation of lower energy bonds like those of some PTMs including phosphorylations.
source: Ultraviolet photodissociation (UVPD) using 193 nm photons is an alternative to existing collision- and electron-based activation methods in proteomic mass spectrometry. This method energizes peptide ions via a single absorption event of high-energy photons resulting in a greater number of diagnostic fragment ions and the conservation of lower energy bonds like those of some PTMs including phosphorylations (Brodbelt, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature describing the UVPD method.

claim: UVPD results in better certainty in PTM localization and conservation of PTMs.
